name: Humidifier
lead: A humidifier is an appliance that adds water vapour or fine droplets to indoor air to raise its relative humidity. Point-of-use models serve a single room, such as a bedroom, while whole-house units connect to a building's heating system [1]. Humidifiers are also built into some medical ventilators for patient comfort [1].

In skin care and looksmaxxing, bedroom humidifiers are used on the idea that dry, heated winter air dries and tightens the skin. Wikipedia notes that indoor humidity can fall to roughly 10 to 20 percent in winter when cold outside air is heated, and that a relative humidity of 30 to 50 percent is generally recommended for homes [1].

Research specific to bedroom humidifiers and facial appearance is sparse. Laboratory work has examined how low humidity affects the barrier function of cultured epidermal cells [2], and clinical literature on humidification deals mainly with respiratory care and neonatal skin. Poorly maintained units can spread microorganisms, and overuse can encourage mould and dust mites [1].

paras: Evaporative or wick humidifiers consist of a reservoir, a wick and a fan; because evaporation falls as room humidity rises, they are partly self-regulating [1]. Wicks can grow mould if they are not fully dried between fillings and accumulate mineral deposits over time [1].

Impeller humidifiers fling water at a diffuser to create fine droplets and are usually louder than other types [1]. Ultrasonic humidifiers use a vibrating ceramic diaphragm to produce a cool fog of droplets about one micron across; because the droplets carry whatever is in the tank, mineral impurities from hard water can settle as a sticky white dust, and microorganisms growing in a stagnant tank can be dispersed into the air [1].

Steam or warm-mist humidifiers use a heating element. Wikipedia notes that boiled water is less likely than a cool mist to carry minerals or microorganisms, but that boiling uses more energy and poorly designed heaters can overheat [1]. Some units include demineralisation cartridges, activated charcoal filters, ultraviolet lamps or ionisers [1]. Furnace-installed designs include bypass drum, disc wheel, flow-through and spray-mist types [1]. Simple homemade evaporators using a bowl and towel are also described [1].

Raising ambient humidity is proposed to slow evaporation of water from the skin surface, so that the outer layer retains more moisture. Wikipedia states that low humidity can contribute to dermatitis, dry mucous membranes and dry eyes, though its statements are summary-level [1]. A 2025 laboratory study used a reconstructed human epidermis model to examine how low humidity affects keratinocyte barrier function [2].
No clinical trial found in the sources reviewed tests a bedroom humidifier against facial skin appearance, wrinkles or acne in healthy adults.

Related research includes the 2025 reconstructed-epidermis experiment noted above, which is a laboratory model and not a human trial [2]. Clinical humidification research is largely respiratory: a meta-analysis of 27 randomized trials with 8,876 patients compared humidified with non-humidified low-flow oxygen, and its abstract reports less bacterial contamination of humidifier bottles with non-humidified oxygen [3]. A review of infant skin care notes that humidified incubators help prevent dehydration in babies born with collodion membranes [4]. In a small study of 12 men staying in a hotel, a humidifier was used to vaporise hinoki cypress oil, and the authors reported increased natural killer cell activity; the humidifier there was a delivery method for the oil rather than the subject of testing [5].

Wikipedia reports that an indoor relative humidity below about 51 percent was associated with significantly lower mite and allergen levels, and that overuse of a humidifier can raise humidity enough to promote dust mites and mould and can contribute to hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sometimes called humidifier lung [1]. A hygrostat or regular humidity checks are described as ways to avoid excess [1]. A published case report describes humidifier lung as a clinical condition [6].
Ultrasonic models can disperse minerals and pathogens from the tank, and wicks and tanks need regular cleaning [1]. Heated models can pose burn and fire risks if poorly designed [1].

Humidifiers appear in skin-care and sleep-environment discussions as a way to counteract dry winter indoor air alongside moisturisers, though the sources reviewed contain no community-sourced claims to quote. Reported target humidity ranges in popular guidance often match the 30 to 50 percent figure [1], but evidence for a specific optimum for skin is not established in the sources reviewed.

Considerations that retailers and appliance guides list include tank capacity and room size, noise (impeller models are louder [1]), whether the unit has a built-in hygrostat, the availability of demineralisation filters or wicks and their replacement cost (cartridges described at roughly $10 to $15 [1]), and how easily the tank can be cleaned. Room units commonly cost about $30 to $80.
